items.text: A tool to understand Earth’s surface changes by comparing radar observations and explaining their limits.
items.title: What is SurfaceSignal?

items.text: A NASA and ISRO radar mission that observes Earth’s surface.
items.title: What is NISAR?

items.text: Radar sends signals and measures their return. The satellite’s motion helps form surface images.
items.title: How does SAR work?

items.text: Comparing compatible passes reveals where signal intensity changed between two dates.
items.title: Why compare observations?

items.text: More energy returned to the radar. This can have different causes and alone identifies no specific phenomenon.
items.title: What does an increase mean?

items.text: Less energy returned to the radar. A smoother surface is one possible explanation, among others.
items.title: What does a decrease mean?

items.text: We apply explicit intensity and size criteria to valid pixels. These criteria are exploratory.
items.title: How do we identify changes?

items.text: The radar product records return intensity. Differences and areas are calculated from those records.
items.title: What was directly observed?

items.text: It is a hypothesis about what may explain the signal, such as changes in water, vegetation or moisture.
items.title: What is interpretation?

items.text: Different causes can produce similar signals. Independent references aligned in space and time are needed.
items.title: Why is the cause unconfirmed?

items.text: Vegetation, agriculture, moisture and urban areas require additional methods and references. Ground motion needs appropriate products and techniques.
items.title: What could we study next?

items.text: Results are exploratory and lack operational validation. They do not replace official services or emergency guidance.
items.title: Why are these not official alerts?
